description: Little Crow, born in Kaposia, was a dissolute and quarrelsome leader who opposed change in dress and habits, was unfriendly to missionaries, and led the hostile tribes in resistance against white settlers. He was known as a bad Indian and was the chief instigator of the insurrection, though he escaped after the conflict and was later killed by a farmer near Hutchinson. Other Day, a Dakota Indian, was taught to read and write by Americans, found the skills good, and became acquainted with the Sacred Writings, which led him to believe in the Great Spirit’s approval of his conduct. He escaped from evil and arrived with sixty-two men, women, and children, transported from Yellow Medicine to Carver, and played a role in the battle against the Sioux. The pastor, Mr. Noble, delivered stirring speeches supporting the war and was deeply affected by the assassination of the greatest president, showing mental agony during services the Sunday after. The draft was resisted in some counties, and the sale of a strip of land angered the Indians, contributing to tensions.

Two frightened kids, after a fire nearly burned through the floor due to their carelessness, realized they had caused an alarm and never got together, meeting secretly on a back street for over a quarter of a century before finally revealing their ordeal. Capt. William Henry Acker, a respected leader in the Union army, was fatally shot in the forehead by a rebel sharpshooter during the first battle of Bull Run, becoming the only man in his company to receive fatal injuries. He was honored by his comrades, whose deep grief over his death cast a gloom over the unit, inspiring them to retaliate with volleys under the watchword "this for our captain." His funeral on Sunday, May 4, 1862, at St. Paul's Church drew the largest crowd of citizens from St. Paul, Minneapolis, St. Anthony, and Stillwater, reflecting the high esteem in which he was held. The first Grand Army post in St. Paul was named the Acker Post in his honor, recognizing him as a key martyr of Minnesota’s Union cause.

Mr. Goodrich, the state printer, fabricated telegraph messages, including a fake speech falsely attributed to William H. Seward, and used the Pioneer and Minnesotian for distribution, with the Pioneer being delivered at 4 o'clock and distributed citywide. He claimed a right to print both Republican and Democratic proceedings, which were assigned to the Minnesotian and Pioneer respectively. Marshall Robinson worked as a compositor on the Pioneer and later served as state printer for Nevada. W.H. Shelley, once prominent in local Republican circles, switched to the Democratic side after Andrew Johnson's political swing and ran for collector of customs, though his nomination was not confirmed. Frederick Douglass’s lecture in St. Paul sold out the theater, with only standing room available. The contract for printing political proceedings required significant material costs and was awarded to the two leading papers. An Indian attack on a command of 150 men at 4 o'clock resulted in casualties, prompting public denunciations of civil and military authorities.

The levee in St. Paul was a bustling hub where steamers arrived daily, drawing crowds of newspaper messengers, merchants, and residents. Steamers like the Gray Eagle and Itasca, known for their distinctive whistles—deep bass, combination, shriek, and discordant notes—were central to the town’s news distribution. The Gray Eagle departed Dubuque at 9 a.m. and the Itasca from Prairie du Chien at noon, meeting at the river bend and arriving at the levee simultaneously. Both were among the fastest boats and were expected to bring news of the 1858 Atlantic cable laying. Officers of packet companies were regarded as local kings, drawing attention comparable to a major general. Steamers transported news rapidly, especially to Dubuque and Chicago, with messengers scrambling to reach the clerk’s office. James J. Hill and Theodore Borup attended the levee for manifest copies, not to compete with news gatherers. The scene of six or eight steamers at once contrasted sharply with the current levee.

Dan Emmet, a minstrel from Ohio, founded the first traveling minstrel troupe in the U.S. in 1843 and wrote "Dixie," a melody that became a popular Confederate song and later a national tune. He sent a copy of "Dixie" to R.C. Munger in St. Paul, who believed it would be a hit and financially supported its publication; the first performance of "Dixie" in the West occurred at Munger Bros' music store in New York. Emmet was indifferent to his brother Lafayette S. Emmett, chief justice of Minnesota, who had two "t"s in his name while Emmet used only one. Andrew Jackson Morgan, a printer-politician and Jacksonian Democrat from St. Paul, resembled Stephen A. Douglas and carried a silver dollar claimed to have been given by Andrew Jackson; he died in Ohio over forty years ago from an overdose of hilarity. Loyal Kentuckians celebrated a victory against rebel invaders from Tennessee, Mississippi, and Alabama, expressing gratitude to neighbors from Minnesota, Indiana, and Ohio.

The battle of Mill Springs resulted in Confederate losses of 600 killed, wounded, and prisoners, and Union losses of 248 killed and wounded. Union forces captured 12 cannons, 200 wagons, ammunition, supplies, and camp equipment. Col. Fry, in a border incident, shot a stranger he believed to be a Confederate sympathizer, later confirmed to be General Zollicoffer, who had pointed to Union forces and claimed they were his men. The victory broke up the Confederate right flank, opened a path into East Tennessee, and forced Gen. Johnston’s withdrawal from Bowling Green to Nashville. Peyton, a Unionist from Tennessee, was mocked as a "hoop-skirt" convert and received a hoop skirt from Southern ladies, prompting him to join the Confederate cause. He later died in his first battle due to recklessness. Confederate leaders revised their view of Union fighting strength after the battle. The Pioneer Guards, a ceremonial unit, was noted for its appearance and lack of combat readiness. No one knew who shot Peyton, though Col. Fry shot Zollicoffer.

George W. Moore was a long-serving editor and publisher of the Pioneer Press, serving continuously with the merged paper except during his volunteer service in the Civil War. He held the position of collector of the port of St. Paul from 1861 to over twenty years later, appointed by President Lincoln. He was a staunch Democrat, a candidate for governor, and a key figure in the early newspaper industry in the Northwest. He sold his interest in the Minnesotian to Dr. Foster in 1860 and was given the printing of the legislature’s journals as part payment, severing ties with the paper he helped found. Frank Moore, born in Tioga County, Pennsylvania, came to St. Paul with his brother and worked at the Pioneer Press for over forty years, eventually becoming head of the composing room. Dr. Foster, editor of the Minnesotian and a Republican power, denounced Gov. Sibley, arguing that state bonds were illegal and would never pay principal or interest. The rivalry between the Minnesotian and the St. Paul Daily Press ended when Foster surrendered the printing plant to its projectors.

Visitors from Cincinnati, Chicago, and Milwaukee arrived at St. Paul’s lower levee during the summer, marched to the Hall of the Order, and were greeted with a grand banquet. Among them were Alf. Burnett of Cincinnati, a celebrated elocutionist, and Gov. Alexander Randall of Wisconsin. The visitors wore long black robes resembling prisoners, and the following day were feasted at Minnehaha Falls. A.M. Carver, a prominent printer and actor at the St. Paul Times, was acclaimed for his portrayal of Uncle Tom in *Uncle Tom’s Cabin*. The Sons of Malta, a secret order organized in an Eastern state and expanding rapidly across the West, enrolled merchants, lawyers, doctors, printers, and half the male population. They originated a scheme involving bouncing candidates into the air, considered one of their mildest atrocities. Jebb, a reporter for the Times, published a report of a chicken theft and hurled a papal excommunication at the thief, ending his career. Merchants stocked goods from November to April due to winter shipping costs. The hotel known as the Merchants no longer exists in its original form.

H.O. Bassford is one of the best-known printers in the Northwest, having served as printer, reporter, editor, publisher, and type founder, and remains active despite nearly fifty years in the industry. Jacob T. McCoy was a skilled typist and singer who served as a private in the Second Minnesota, rising to first lieutenant, and now resides in Meadeville, Pa. George W. Armstrong, known as the "Beau Brummel" of early printers, wore kid gloves and was elected state treasurer in 1857 before turning to real estate. George W. Benedict was a genial foreman of the old St. Paul Press and is now editor and publisher of the Sauk Rapids Sentinel. Edward Richards, a foreman of the Pioneer and Minnesotian before and after the war, served as a soldier and correspondent during the darkest days of the rebellion, later becoming collector of customs at St. Paul under Presidents Garfield and Arthur. The rebellion involved significant military actions, including a retreat under night and a confrontation with Gen. Grant, and several printers, including Bassford, McCoy, and Benedict, survived and remained active in the printing industry.

President Lincoln expressed congratulations to Minnesota regiments, with the Second Minnesota receiving recognition for valor at Mill Springs and a silk flag from Louisville mayor J.M. Dolph, who praised their service in subduing rebel invaders. The Minnesota legislature honored the state’s soldiers, noting the bravery of both victorious and defeated regiments, and affirmed their pride and honor. Rev. Frederick A. Noble, pastor of the House of Hope church, was a prominent, eloquent, and aggressive preacher whose ideal statesman was Lincoln. Gen. McClellan, once admired as the army’s idol, made frequent trips to St. Paul and ordered the Hutchinson family out of the Army of the Potomac for abolitionist sentiments, though by war’s end, the army widely chanted John Brown’s song. Gen. Grant was briefly arrested by McClellan for consulting with Gen. Buell without permission, an order halted by the War Department. The Army of the Potomac suffered a defeat at Bull Run, while Grant’s army at Pittsburg Landing was more demoralized, and the Civil War entered a gloomy period in 1862.

The president, during a period of economic hardship between 1857 and 1861 marked by low wages and absent money, called for 600,000 men, with Minnesota supplying five regiments. A conspiracy intended to murder the president, vice president, and cabinet, resulting in only one fatality—Secretary of State Seward, whose death deeply moved the audience. The president later allowed only 38 executions in 1862 after receiving remonstrances. Mrs. Stella Selby led the Ladies Aid Society, which met to sew for wounded soldiers and assist refugees, while Miss M.O. Holyoke, known as Clara Barton of Minnesota, collected sanitary supplies. Mrs. Bartlett Presley was a devoted supporter of the fire department, providing coffee and sandwiches during cold nights, and was remembered as a noble woman. The president delivered a powerful invocation before being assassinated, stating, "With malice towards none and with charity to all, and with firmness for the right, as God gives us to see the right." A prize fight in England and the Democratic convention in Charleston were topics of public conversation, reflecting societal preoccupations.

William Jebb was a prominent debater known for his command of language and fluency of speech, often entertaining weary distributors with his eloquence. On the first day of the battle at Pittsburg Landing, 6,000 fresh recruits, having never heard musketry, fled when the enemy approached and hid on the river bank, unable to be moved by command or persuasion. Gen. Buell arrived and threatened to fire on them, but it had no effect. The battle, sometimes called the Battle of Shiloh near the Church of Shiloh, saw intense fighting with a terrible slaughter in Union forces due to misunderstandings of orders, lack of cooperation between subordinates and superiors, and the inexperience of recruits. The enemy attacked the left wing, aiming to break through, create panic, and cut off retreat, but their fire was weak and they began to withdraw. Gen. Halleck, who commanded over 100,000 well-equipped men and was compared to the king of France, was expected to deliver a crushing blow but failed to do so. After the battle, Halleck took personal command, placing Grant second in command.

The Civil War saw significant military setbacks for the Union, including General McClellan’s retreat from Richmond and General Pope’s defeats, while Union armies in the West made no progress toward the Confederacy’s heart. Rebel marauders devastated Kentucky and Ohio, and privateers escaped to Europe with cotton and returned with arms and ammunition to support the Confederacy. France planned to invade Mexico to establish a monarchical government, and European powers (except Russia) expressed sympathy for the South. Rumors of foreign intervention were widespread, and enemies of the government worked to prevent enlistment and spread disease. In England, an improved fire engine was patented at the close of the 17th century, featuring an oak cistern, pump, air chamber, and strong leather suction pipe with a spiral metal piece. In Minnesota, Indians threatened a village near New Ulm, prompting home guards to be formed, though authorities lacked arms or ammunition. The St. Paul Press faced backlash for supporting war efforts, leading to threats and the formation of a self-defense company led by Capt. E.R. Otis. A typo in a news article falsely claimed the Battle of Mill Springs as the first Union victory and named a rebel general as killed.

Wabasha, a Sioux chief, was executed despite not killing or injuring any white man or participating in the plunder of property, and he was not found guilty of massacres of women and children, though he was probably involved in all major battles. His wife and children were left in the care of the speaker, and he instructed them not to grieve, emphasizing that brave people should meet death as a Dakotah would. Rattling Runner, his son-in-law, claimed Wabasha deceived him about surrendering, affirming his own innocence. Condemned prisoners, interviewed by Rev. S.R. Riggs, claimed innocence and expressed hope in salvation. Judge Flandrau led families to safety during the outbreak, evacuating towns as outlaws burned nearly 200 houses and committed atrocities including rape, murder, and captivity. Wabasha County and Wabasha Street in St. Paul are named after his father. After execution, his bodies were transported to a sandbar in front of the city and dumped. J.Q.A. Ward married Miss Pratt under unusual circumstances, a union that caused town commotion and ended in divorce without cohabitation.

Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1, organized in November 1854 under the city charter, was the first full-fledged fire organization in St. Paul and is credited as the "Father of the Volunteer Fire Department of St. Paul" due to John McCloud's initiative. It adopted a constitution and by-laws, with members agreeing to respond promptly to fire alarms. The organization provided excusal from jury duty, poll tax, road work, and state military service for five years. It had insufficient equipment, leading to petitions for two approved fire engines and a central cistern for water supply, which were fulfilled by 1858. The company participated in the Paul Fire Department’s first parade on September 12, 1859, alongside three other companies totaling 175 men. Rev. John Penman joined after being induced by a member, but he later published an exposé in Harper's Weekly exposing the organization’s secret activities, causing public backlash. John McCloud and Thompson Ritchie purchased the first fire engine introduced in the Northwest, which aided pioneer merchants. The organization’s property was later transferred to the city in 1856 due to financial difficulties.

Col. Bailie Peyton, a member of the Fifth Regiment Louisiana Volunteer National Guards, was presented with a sword by citizens of New Orleans at the outbreak of the Mexican War, which he carried throughout the conflict. The sword, inscribed "Presented to Col. Bailie Peyton, Fifth Regiment Louisiana Volunteer National Guards, by his friends of New Orleans. His country required his services. His deeds will add glory to her arms," has a historic record tied to his service. Peyton's sword was carried during the war, and he was designated by Gen. Scott to receive the surrender of the City of Mexico when Santa Anna surrendered. Capt. E.Y. Shelly, born in Bucks County, PA, joined the Third United States Dragoons upon the war's outbreak and participated in battles at Palo Alto, Monterey, and Buena Vista, where the American forces were successful against Mexican forces led by Santa Ana. The government issued resolutions pledging support to citizens, calling on young men to enlist, and promising financial aid to dependant families. After the war, the Third Dragoons were mustered out in St. Louis. Lieut. Tuttle currently possesses Peyton's sword, and there has been ongoing correspondence about returning it to Peyton's relatives, with no resolution reached.

Tom Marshall, a prominent Kentucky orator and Whig who supported Bell and Everett, was known for his eloquence and was from a slave state. While sauntering down Third Street, he met the Little Giants, who halted before him and demanded a speech, believing he would not criticize their leader. Marshall delivered a lecture on Napoleon in the Concert Hall, which stood twenty-five feet back from the sidewalk and had multiple stories, with a tailor shop on the river side. The Wide Awakes and Little Giants were uniformed political organizations active in 1860 to attract voter attention. The Minnesotian office hosted events involving the Wide Awakes and received black Republican whisky as payment for a bad debt, which it could not sell or distribute. A detail was sent to Fort Ridgely to bury the dead and rescue the wounded. The Little Giants were invited to the Minnesotian office to reduce the supply of black Republican whisky, which was consumed enthusiastically, demonstrating the principle of "love rum and hate <DW65>s." A fire rapidly engulfed the Concert Hall, killing Charles and August Mueller, who did not realize their lives were in danger. Under the sidewalk, flammable materials were stored, and the fire was first noticed there.

Fort Ridgely, a poorly defended fort with only two or three stone and several wooden buildings, was surrounded by 700 to 800 armed Sioux and besieged for several days with only two assaults. It was commanded by Lieut. T.J. Sheehan, who led 150 soldiers, 50 Rangers, and civilians, including 300 refugees. The outbreak began at Redwood and spread rapidly, driving settlers from their homes and causing widespread desolation. The Sioux, hereditary enemies of the Chippewas, were feared to have cooperated in an indiscriminate massacre, though a Chippewa chief, Hole-in-the-Day, attacked Sioux near Shakopee, killing 15–20. The governor called an extra session of the legislature to arm volunteers and assist refugees, issuing a proclamation against lawlessness. Little Six and Medicine Bottle, two Sioux chiefs involved in the outbreak, were arrested, tried, and executed at Fort Snelling in front of 10,000 people—making them the last Native Americans to receive capital punishment. The Sioux forfeited 750,000 acres and an annual annuity of $68,000 due to their actions.

The Mansion House, a three-story frame building erected by Nicholas Pottgieser on the corner of Wabasha and Fifth Streets at a cost of $12,000, was a popular resort for weary travelers who received a hearty welcome. In 1866, guest Hawkes accidentally shot and killed his young and beautiful wife during a stay. The Cosmopolitan Hotel, a four-story frame building on Summit Avenue and St. Peter Street, was well patronized and burned in a fire on May 19, 1878, which was caused by incendiaries and resulted in a loss of $20,000, partially insured. Flames spread rapidly, consuming eastern and southern rooms and collapsing walls; a lady named McClellan was burned to death. The fire also destroyed many frame buildings on the opposite side of the street. Warren Carpenter’s hotel, located on Summit Avenue and Ramsey Street, was built by him with dreams of millions but was burned to the ground on January 26, 1879, after passing beyond his control. Charles Mueller and his brother jumped from a window to escape flames during a fire, survived, and recovered; August Mueller remains living in the city. Spectators often relieved firemen from working on brakes, though police were sometimes needed to enforce compliance.

Paul, a prominent figure in St. Paul, was involved in journalism, law, and civic organizations, including commanding the Wide-Awakes in 1860 to promote Abraham Lincoln’s candidacy. He delivered messages ahead of the regular mail, gaining an advantage over competitors, and reported on frontier incidents involving savages. Paul studied law under Hon. Edmund Rice and later worked at the Bank of Minnesota, established by ex-Gov. Marshall. Gov. Marshall, a noble man, initially reported a Union defeat at the First Battle of Bull Run but later affirmed the country’s recovery and became known for defending national honor. Mr. Winslow owned a telegraph line in Paul, New Canada, and Rose and Reserve townships, refusing to share election results, which caused public frustration and a stormy confrontation with Gov. Marshall, after which the Press received full telegraphic reports and retained them. From 1854 to 1860, the St. Paul newspapers competed fiercely over publishing the president’s message, with the Times initially using a fake report from the Minnesotian. The Winslow hotel, built in 1854, was a key location, visited by William H. Seward in 1860. Paul’s involvement in the Wide-Awakes and civic life foreshadowed his untimely death, which was linked to the success of Lincoln’s cause.

Irvine Hall, a three-story, three-cornered building at Third Street and Seven Corners, was a popular amusement hall in St. Paul, known as Melodeon Hall. It hosted minstrel companies in 1857 and 1858, including Dan Emmet’s troupe with Frank Lombard, Max Irwin, and Johnny Ritter. Max Irwin gained fame in 1858 for a performance where he rushed to the stage with a carpetbag and kissed the entire troupe, an act that became a sensation. Johnny Martin, a red-headed Irishman and foreman of the Daily Minnesotian, responded immediately to fire bells and celebrated after each fire by declaring his duty to kill an Irishman, though he never found one. De Witt C. Cooley, a witty political figure, gained attention at a Democratic meeting by calling for "Holler for Cooley," though his speech failed when an audience member mocked the irony. The hall hosted distinguished speakers like Edward Everett, Ralph Waldo Emerson, and John B. Gough. Cable laying attempts occurred in 1857, 1858, 1863, and succeeded in 1865. A celebration in St. Paul on September 1, 1858, honored the Atlantic cable’s laying, which took two or three days to reach the city due to lack of telegraphy.

James M. Goodhue arrived in St. Paul in 1849 from Lancaster, Wisconsin, with a Washington hand press and fonts of type to start a newspaper, accompanying two young printers, Ditmarth and Dempsey. The Daily North Star was launched in the state capital by H.H. Young, former editor of the Henderson Independent, as a Breckinridge-supporting "bread and butter paper" that did not require Associated Press dispatches, a perfecting press, or linotype machines. In contrast, early printing, such as for the Sunday Pioneer Press, relied on 600 hand presses, 600 pressmen, 600 boys, and 5,000 compositors due to the absence of stereotyping, resulting in one-dollar papers with minimal profit. After the 1859 election, rival Republican offices campaigned for the state printer position, needing financial support and facing a patronage division issue. In 1860, the first telegraph line reached St. Paul, but high costs prevented the three St. Paul papers from accessing Associated Press news; a secret contract by the Pioneer excluded the Minnesotian and Times, who waited until the Pioneer was published. Stereotyping was introduced in 1880, and linotype machines were installed in 1892. Robert V. Hesselgrave worked in various St. Paul offices. The Daily North Star is noted as a historically overlooked paper.

The amendment, passed by an immense majority with strong community support, was promoted as providing employment to thousands and stimulating economic speculation through the promise of extraordinary returns. Though supported by leading men from both parties, Republicans later sought political advantage from it, and the Minnesotian, edited by Dr. Thomas Foster, opposed it with criticism that had the opposite effect of intended. A military tribunal from September 30 to November 5 found 321 individuals guilty, sentencing 303 to death. John W. Sickels, a young reporter from an Eastern city and member of the Times editorial staff, provided a graphic account of events, concluding he could not determine the origin of the difficulty—a statement seen as humorous by old inhabitants. The amendment's passage sparked public outcry in Eastern cities over claims of a wholesale slaughter of Native Americans. Reporters covered the conflict, remaining on site for several days. Business was suspended the day after the events, and daily papers were not issued.

Governor Sibley faced significant conflict over bond issuance for railroad companies, which demanded funds under a law granting $10,000 per mile for graded roads. After railroad companies refused to accept state-imposed restrictions, the Supreme Court issued a peremptory writ ordering bond issuance, prompting Sibley to reluctantly comply despite believing the court lacked authority to coerce the executive branch. The bonds failed to sell on the New York market, leading to disappointment, humiliation, and the collapse of the railway construction scheme, with railroad companies defaulting and the state’s credit damaged. The Minnesotian newspaper, which criticized bond issuance and was feared to reflect community sentiment, faced an injunction preventing its business manager from drawing state funds; the district court later ruled in its favor, and the supreme court confirmed the decision. The "Five Million Loan Election" drew intense public interest, with St. Paul, a city of 10,000, voting overwhelmingly in favor of the law.

Capt. Shelly, a modest and patriotic Minnesotan, organized a company with Major Brackett, forming Brackett's Battalion in September 1861. The battalion, composed of three Minnesota companies, was initially assigned to the Curtis Horse and later to the Fifth Iowa Cavalry. It served at Fort Donelson in February 1862, where it prevented Confederate Gen. Buckner from receiving reinforcements despite not being in the main battle, and again in August 1862 during a minor rebel attack led by Forrest and Wheeler. A third attack in February 1863 ended in retreat, leaving many Confederate dead. The regiment performed guard, picket, and scout duty, enduring long periods without food or sleep. Brackett's Battalion was the only Minnesota unit engaged at Fort Donelson. After Chickamauga, it was stationed on the dividing line between opposing forces. Most of Shelly’s men reinlisted on January 1, 1864, and returned home on a thirty-day furlough. Shelly was mustered out in spring 1865 and remained engaged in printing, having been the first printer to permanently locate in Minnesota.

On a stormy night in December 1863, a fire broke out in a hotel on Jackson and Seventh Streets, spreading rapidly despite a porter's attempt to extinguish it with water. Dense smoke filled the halls, rendering breathing nearly impossible and causing panic among over two hundred guests, most of whom were asleep and unaware of the danger. The fire department arrived too late, as the bitterly cold weather froze their hoses, and they abandoned efforts to save the building, instead focusing on rescuing guests. Four of six or eight buildings were destroyed; valuable items like pianos, furniture, and pictures were thrown into the street and snow. Pete O'Brien, the night watchman, recognized the risk of a panic. Thieves stole jewelry and clothing. The incident was linked to two boys and kids who, after obtaining a key to the representative hall, engaged in revelry and smoking before returning it, causing a fire that led to an alarm. The doctor, who saw the fire news in the Chicago Tribune, became enraged and rushed out into the street, cursing the president. No lives were lost, though there were narrow escapes.

The narrator, a young student, gained a reputation as a speller after correctly spelling "phthisic" at four schools, earning recognition as the champion speller of four districts and ensuring their name was never last called. Though considered too young for joint spelling matches, they secretly rode in a four-horse sleigh to a grand spelling contest four miles from their village, where they watched as two top spellers selected sides—neither from their school. The narrator’s school was recognized for producing the district’s best speller. Meanwhile, military authorities faced challenges transporting supplies to frontier troops due to the lack of railroads, relying on wagon teams. A squad seized Gov. Ramsey’s carriage team, sending it to Abercrombie with supplies for the fort. The old man, refusing to leave his son, stayed at the press until the paper was printed, while others, like Mr. Metcalf, searched for him. A team was also seen tied behind a house near a bridge, believed safe until the owner returned.

The Republicans campaigned vigorously in 1858 to secure state and legislative offices, including the governorship and U.S. Senate seat, with speakers Hon. Galusha A. Grow and Hon. Schuyler Colfax delivering speeches at the Old People's Theater on the corner of Fourth and St. Peter Streets. The theater was packed and Grow’s speech lasted an hour, followed by Colfax’s ten-minute address, after which a fire alarm was sounded, leading to the theater’s rapid destruction. Church sextons rang bells for fifteen minutes in response to the alarm, causing widespread panic and movement between uptown and downtown areas. On the night of the 1860 presidential election, Republicans gathered at a concert hall to hear returns, with singing surpassing news from four precincts. The Greenman House, located on Fifth and St. Peter Streets, was burned by John Summers, its owner. A fire alarm also triggered a response from fire companies, who reported to engine houses; a doctor was later heard beneath rubble, criticizing the fire department’s delay.

Hon. Michael E. Ames, a prominent figure in St. Paul’s early legal fraternity, had a more enviable reputation than anyone else, known for his punctiliousness and imperturbability. During a fire in his uppertown apartment, he opened the window and, in a supplicating manner, requested firemen to halt operations to complete his toilet, escaping unharmed while his apartment was destroyed. Gen. W.T. Sherman commanded the Department of the Cumberland and oversaw the movement of the Second Minnesota to Louisville, where they were directed to Lebanon Junction. Sherman was involved in intense fighting at Shiloh and was shot twice—once in the hand, once in the shoulder—with a ball cutting his coat and passing through his hat; horses were also shot. Sherman intervened to prevent Gen. Grant from resigning after a near-fatal injury, an action later proven wise. Bishop Willoughby, a well-known early figure, was mistakenly reported as administering confirmation when it was actually Bishop Whipple. Halleck was ordered to Washington, and Grant was made commander of the Department of West Tennessee with headquarters in Memphis. Sherman met Halleck during this period.

Mr. Stuart, originally from Detroit, was hired by the Minnesotian printer in the spring of 1858 after distributing two cases of type, which astonished colleagues. He set 2,000 ems of solid bourgeois type per hour and maintained this rate throughout the day, earning a reputation as a rapid compositor whose skill spread throughout the city. In 1862, he enlisted in the Eighth Regiment, serving three years before returning home as a lieutenant. He was also a forceful writer and expert in printing business, later publishing a paper in Sault Ste. Marie, where he died. E.S. Lightbourn, another printer, served three years in the Seventh Minnesota and became foreman of the Pioneer after the war. The foreman paid every person employed, including himself and the devil, $2.50 in gold, and printers were notified for a typographical struggle. Mr. Stuart’s composition of 23,000 ems was the most remarkable feat in the region. William A. Hill came to St. Paul in the 1850s and was a member of the Seventh Minnesota.

Bridge Square was a central location in St. Paul, housing the old Press building, where the narrator slept on a lounge overlooking the square, with guns and ammunition stored under their bed. The area hosted Agony Hall, one of the city’s first free concert halls, possibly named for its agonizing music or beverages. The old Press building, originally a banking house built by Mackubin & Edgerton, was later leased to Bechtner & Kottman and remodeled into a hotel. In 1869, the Press moved to a new building on Third and Minnesota streets. Earle S. Goodrich, editor of the Pioneer, entered the composing room and set the first type in the new building without copy, earning praise for the clean editorial. A bitter conflict existed between editors Dr. Foster and Thomas M. Newson (referred to as Mr. Timothy Muggins Newson), with their hostile relations persisting until the legislature adjourned, after which their partnership dissolved. General Grant, during a cavalry charge, observed enemy forces dropping provisions and luggage to escape with guns, noting that an immediate pursuit could have captured prisoners and some guns.

A battle fought near Shakopee in May 1858 involved the Sioux and Chippewas. Ex-Gov. Sibley, familiar with Indian character, commanded troops assembled at St. Peter who began offensive operations against the Sioux with minimal supplies and ununiformed units. Nelson's division arrived from Savannah by steamers, proceeded to the left wing, and were regarded as veterans who earned confidence the battle would end successfully. The First Battery, the only Minnesota unit engaged, had its first combat experience and limited drill time before receiving guns and horses weeks prior. Despite being unprepared, it performed bravely under fire, dislodging rebel batteries placed in the timber at the far end of the field and earning warm commendation from the commanding officer. Its actions at critical moments convinced the rebels they had encountered a foe worthy of their steel. Two or three days after the battle, the Second Minnesota sent letters claiming they shot Bailie Peyton and Gen. Zollicoffer, who had made a defiant speech promising to take his troops to Indiana or go to hell, but did not go to Indiana.

In 1862, a revolt erupted among the Sioux, triggered by grievances over unfair treatment by traders, lack of accounting knowledge, and being forced to pay debts before readiness. Indians, including those from Little Six’s band, murdered several people in Action, Meeker County, and fled to Redwood, marking the start of widespread violence. The revolt led to the killing of 1,000 people, destruction of millions in property, and homelessness for 30,000. A secret organization among tepee Indians aimed to declare war on whites. Company B of the Fifth Regiment, under Captain Marsh, was sent to respond but was ambushed and lost about 25 members, including Marsh. The massacre began on August 18th. The balance of condemned Indians were confined until spring, then transported by steamer to Davenport and later to a point on the Missouri River, where they were allowed to sow discontent that eventually led to the Custer massacre. The St. Paul Weekly Journal, edited by Dr. Massey, opposed the war prosecution and existed briefly in 1862. Government officers were criticized for neglecting responsibilities and preventing a planned warm reception for the condemned Indians by having the steamer Favorite pass through St. Paul at midnight.

The Old Frame Building, constructed in 1850 on the southeast corner of Third and Exchange streets, was built by the Elfelt Brothers, who occupied the ground floor as a dry goods store. The building is one of the city's oldest structures and featured a hall that served as a principal amusement venue. A room on its second story was later fitted up and became the beginning of the St. Paul library, established after a social and supper event in February 1861, organized by the ladies of Protestant churches with aid from the Young Men's Christian Association. The building's Exchange Street side bore the Elfelt Brothers' name until recently. In a significant meeting presided over by Hon. John S. Prince, Hon. John M. Gilman, an honored resident and former Democratic candidate for congress, delivered remarks in hearty sympathy with the meeting's objective, receiving strong approval. Hon. J.W. Taylor followed Gilman with a strong speech in favor of supporting Mr. Lincoln, who regarded "Dixie" as a national property by capture. The building also housed the Minnehaha Engine Company No. 2, which was organized in winter 1857–1858.

Rebel forces, approaching in overwhelming numbers, launched repeated assaults on Union lines, attempting to find a weak point and avoid the extreme left wing. Despite being repulsed with heavy losses from canister fire at close range, they maintained rapid and vigorous firing, comparable to the most intense hours of the previous day. The Second Minnesota, positioned in the center and exposed to the heaviest enemy fire, engaged in hand-to-hand combat, ran guns through fences, and were the first to use the bayonet, earning enthusiastic praise. The Union forces, under the presence and direction of Generals Grant, Buell, Nelson, and Crittenden, maintained steady fire and coordinated movements, including a new strike. General Grant, despite a sprained ankle, rode continuously from division to division, giving directions throughout the engagement. The fight began at 8:30, with the second line preparing for the enemy advance. At 5 o'clock, rebel firing ceased as their lines fell back half a mile, and a retreat followed, marked by considerable disorder and loss of baggage. Firing resumed before the retreat, prompting the Fifteenth Mississippi and Sixteenth Alabama to recognize the strength of the Minnesotans.

Mr. Moore was half of the carrier staff for the Minnesotian, responsible for delivering newspapers across St. Paul above Wabasha Street, up to College Avenue and Ramsey Street, with Seventh Street as a western limit. He met steamers when they whistled, retrieved bundles of newspapers, and delivered them to the office where editors received telegraph news. As business manager of the Minnesotian, he purchased a Hoe press, type, and a Hoe proof press, the latter still in use at the Pioneer Press. The Athenaeum, built in 1859 by the German Reading Society, served as St. Paul’s only amusement hall with a stage and drop curtain and hosted Plunkett’s Dramatic Company (featuring Susan Denin) shortly before the small opera house on Wabasha Street was built. The Linden Theatrical Company, also performing there, suffered heavily in the Cosmopolitan Hotel fire. The year 1859 was significant in Minnesota’s political history. Aromory Hall, built on Third Street between Cedar and Minnesota in 1859, was used by the Pioneer Guards until the war.

The people of St. Paul were frequently called upon to assist in transporting refugees via boats on the Minnesota River to their place of destination. They watched with great interest the small skirmish at Pittsburgh Landing, where thousands were killed and wounded. The battle, though minor compared to other engagements the Second Minnesota participated in, saw Gen. Zollicoffer killed. The Second Minnesota regiment, which included two full companies recruited in St. Paul and many St. Paulites in other units, suffered 12 killed and 35 wounded. Among the casualties, one name was especially cherished by the people of St. Paul, as much as Ellsworth was cherished by the people of Chicago.

The Daniels House, located on Eagle Street near Seven Corners, was the site of the first hotel fire of any importance in 1852. The building, recently finished and furnished, was destroyed by a strong wind, and local firemen, including Rev. D.D. Neill, Isaac Markley, Bartlett Presley, and W.M. Stees, were unable to save it, though they assisted in saving some furniture. The Sintominie Hotel, located on Sixth and John Streets, was the second hotel to burn, constructed by C.W. Borup and considered the pride of lower town; it was destroyed before opening, with Howard Ward and E.C. Rich preparing to open it. The Winslow House, located in Seven Corners, was also destroyed in a fire, with a few pieces of furniture saved. The Rice House, on Third Street near Market, was the first brick building in St. Paul, constructed by Henry M. Rice, and burned in the winter of 1856; it hosted sessions of the territorial legislature and supreme court. All these fires occurred during St. Paul's early history.

The Old Opera House in St. Paul, built on the site now occupied by the Grand Block and finished in 1866–67, opened with a grand entertainment featuring local talent. It hosted large audiences who gathered to hear speeches by Henry Ward Beecher, Frederick Douglass, Wendell Phillips, Theodore Tilton, and many others from its stage. The parquet area had seats and boxes sold at auction, with Philbrick, a visitor from St. Paul who brought seven or eight people, bidding $72 for a seat and being rumored to be a duke. He later vanished as mysteriously as he appeared and was identified as Coal Oil Johnny, who was out on a lark. The Macfarland Dramatic Company was the first regular company to perform there, with Emily Melville as its chief attraction.

The initiation ritual is described as grand, gloomy, and peculiar, involving a gauntlet that ensures a victim seeks another after their ordeal. When a candidate is proposed, the lodge acts as a committee of investigation. The candidate is examined by the high priest in the secret chamber, where they believe their confession is private but later discover it is shared with full membership. The candidate is questioned by the Grand Commander about support for the acquisition of the Island of Cuba, responding positively, and about lying awake at night and stealing into the enemy's camp, indicating willingness to act in invasion scenarios. Occasionally, the candidate confesses to being a more serious transgressor than expected. The ritual emphasizes loyalty, secrecy, and moral accountability through intense psychological and behavioral testing.

The Okons, descendants of sea kings from the bogs of Tipperary, hold absolute power in the city, controlling every office and remaining as fixed as the stars. They are revered as a stabilizing force, and inciting their displeasure leads to downfall. The paleface, supported by the Okons, rules from a magnificent building, with the Okons never being dislodged. Jack Ward, a bright but self-destructive business manager of the Minnesotian, created the first immigration pamphlet in the territory and married his employer’s daughter after only half an hour of ballroom acquaintance. An old man named Metcalf, over eighty years old and father of T.M. Metcalf, came to the office to assist, setting 1,000 ems before the paper went to press. Threats to throw the office into the river did not materialize. The voyageur returns from a philanthropic visit to the red man, observing a transformation where cultivated fields replace the hostile warrior, and the same bluffs and river remain unchanged.

Col. Marshall of the Seventh Regiment and Col. Uline of the Second Regiment were selected as candidates for a sword contest, driven by public interest. Col. Uline won the sword, receiving over two thousand votes in a single bundle during the final five minutes of voting, supported by numerous friends and a representative at the voting booth. Col. Marshall was backed by friends in various newspaper offices. The Seventh Regiment remained at camp for six weeks, though rumors of night attacks by Confederates persisted. A train incident during the Second Regiment’s move to Lebanon, Ky., involved gunfire, and after a battle, relatives and friends sought information about the men involved. Col. Uline, previously a fireman, was popular with young men in St. Paul. A group of guards, during a train journey, painted their faces, wore Indian costumes, and charged through the camp, yelling the Indian war hoop. The people of St. Paul felt safe from Sioux raids only after the Battle of Wood Lake. Frank H. Pratt, an officer in the Seventh Regiment, later worked in mercantile business in St. Paul.

In 1860, Republican statesmen including W.H. Seward, John P. Hale, Charles Francis Adams, Senator Nye, and General Stewart L. Woodford visited St. Paul to support the Republican presidential candidate. Seward hosted a party attended by these figures. Charles N. Mackubin erected two buildings on the former Metropolitan Hotel site: Mozart Hall at the Third Street end and Masonic Hall at the Fourth Street corner. During the war, Mozart Hall and Masonic Hall hosted a successful winter 1864 sanitary fair benefiting the Sanitary Commission, which raised several thousand dollars from patriotic citizens. The fair included a performance of the cantata "The Haymakers," in which Mrs. Winne, Mrs. Blakeley, and Prof. Perkins took leading roles. The mayor of St. Paul praised firemen as braver than soldiers, causing backlash from the "boys in blue" and city/state press, who perceived him as lacking loyalty; however, he was later re-elected by a large majority. Mr. Miller, a 33rd Degree Mason, received the first recorded midnight funeral service in Masonic Hall.

The floral procession included mounted cadets representing Queen Victoria, President Buchanan, the different States of the Union, and other devices. After Queen Victoria and President Buchanan exchanged lengthy messages, preparations began for a grand celebration in St. Paul. The procession featured military units, civic groups, and cultural organizations, including the Great Western band and O.G. Miller, who was a tenor singer in several St. Paul churches and among the most known printers with musical interests. Early printers, such as Earle S. Goodrich, Thomas Foster, T.M. Newson, and John P. Owens, were also editors and often engaged in discussions of church and state affairs, reflecting the sociability once present in composing rooms. The introduction of the iron printer led to the decline of these traditions, with modern printers no longer receiving state diplomas in the composing room. Printers and actors were often interconnected, as seen in figures like Lawrence Barrett and Stuart Robson, who were both actors and knights of the stick and rule.

The First Minnesota Battery, a light artillery unit organized at Fort Snelling in the fall of 1861 under Captain Emil Munch, earned glory and brought honor to Minnesota by participating in key Civil War campaigns, including the Battle of Pittsburg Landing, the Siege of Vicksburg, the front lines before Atlanta, and the march to the sea. After mustering in, it was sent to St. Louis to receive equipment before moving to Pittsburg Landing, arriving late February 1862. On April 6, it was ordered to the front just before the battle began, where it engaged Confederate forces. During the fighting, a battery opened fire on Union commanders, injuring several, including Maj. Hawkins and Gen. Grant, who lost his sword. The battery later repositioned and inflicted heavy casualties on the rebels. Despite its contributions, it is rarely credited in Minnesota’s Civil War remembrances. The singer, reputedly wealthy, wrote songs including "The Blue and the Gray" and "Good Times for Women," performed in Atlanta six years ago during a suffrage event, and participated in the 11,667th concert. Mr. Hutchinson, appearing in court without an attorney, was deemed capable by the judge after recalling a personal memory.

General Buell was stationed at Columbia, Tennessee, on March 19 with a force of 40,000 men, marching less than five miles a day for nineteen days to reach the Tennessee River, despite being ordered to join Grant's forces urgently. He arrived at Pittsburgh Landing on April 7, where a timely precaution enabled him to save Grant from probable defeat. On that day, a battery was held in reserve. Buell took command of volunteers near Louisville in November 1861, organizing them into divisions and brigades. Judge Charles E. Flandrau, residing in St. Peter, organized a company of volunteers and marched to New Ulm, where he arrived with about 300 poorly armed and inexperienced men. After a desperate encounter, the force lost ten killed and about forty wounded, and the Indians retreated. The enemy in the battle, the Johnnies, fled, leaving dead and dying on a bloody field, with some few surrendering.

The Battle of Pittsburg Landing (April 6–7, 1862) was one of the most devastating engagements of the Civil War, compared to the Battle of Waterloo. Union forces, initially numbering 33,000, lost 1,754 killed, 8,408 wounded, and 2,885 missing, while Confederate forces under Beauregard reported 10,699 total losses. Gen. Pope claimed Gen. Porter was within range of his guns but remained inactive, leading to accusations of disloyalty by Northern newspapers; Porter was court-martialed and dismissed, though Congress later reversed the stigma. Gen. Buell could have prevented heavy casualties by joining Grant earlier but was later tried without public findings. Napoleon Heitz operated a saloon and restaurant where he frequently recounted graphic descriptions of the Battle of Waterloo during meals of Tom and Jerry or oyster stew. The Pioneer moved on July 4, 1863, missing the chance to publish an extra edition due to relocation, coinciding with Gettysburg and Vicksburg’s surrender. In Minnesota, locals opposed Pope’s troop removal request, delaying it until troops completed two marches through the Dakotas to Montana. Hines, a brave supply train traveler, demonstrated skill handling the Sioux force, leading companions to test his courage. Poor soldiers in the South and Dakotas received delicacies collected by noble ladies, which strengthened their health.

General Sibley launched offensive operations in 1861 after gathering about 2,000 men, including the recently paroled Third Regiment and a battery under Captain Mark Hendricks. The expedition marched for two or three days without opposition, then faced a spirited engagement on September 23 near Wood Lake, where 800 men fought an equal number of Indians. After careful caution, Sibley reached Camp Release on September 26, where he found a large Indian camp with 250 mixed-blood individuals and white women and children, having participated in massacres. The camp surrendered, and captives were released. Governor Ramsey attempted to reassure residents by claiming the nearest Indian presence was 80 miles away at Acton, Meeker County, and Fort Ripley was 150 miles distant, though this did not comfort frontiersmen who abandoned their homes and sought protection from the slowly advancing militia. The expedition later moved into the Bad Lands in August 1864, depopulating the region from Fort Ripley to the southern boundary, and encountered Indians multiple times, routing them. Advertisements offered a $25 reward per Sioux scalp. The expedition was documented by city editor J. Fletcher Williams, with illustrations using patent medicine cuts and inverted wood type.

The International Hotel, formerly the Fuller House, was erected in 1856 by A.G. Fuller on the northeast corner of Seventh and Jackson streets. It was a five-story brick building that cost about $110,000 and was the best hotel in the West. Samuel Mayall acquired the property in 1861 and renamed it the International Hotel. The Fuller House was the exception to being the largest hotel in the city, as the Winslow Hotel was the largest, except for the Fuller House. The American House, built in 1849 on Third and Exchange streets, was a landmark and served as a headquarters for territorial politicians, including Generals Pope and Sibley, who issued orders against the rebellious Sioux from there. The American House had peculiar architecture but modern interior fittings. Travelers arriving by steamboat from the Galena, Dunleith, Dubuque and Minnesota Packet Company heard announcements directing them to these hotels. The greatest hotel fire in St. Paul's history occurred on February 3, 1869.

The St. Paul Fire Department, including the Minnehaha Engine Company, Hope Engine Company, and Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company, played a key role in firefighting during the city's early days. On March 16, 1860, a severe fire in a wooden building on Third Street near Jackson destroyed thirty-four buildings, spreading rapidly through two-story frame structures and small houses occupied by store owners. Despite being manned by one hundred men and consisting of three engines and one truck, the department could not contain the flames but successfully cut off the fire’s spread across Robert Street and brought the smouldering mass under control. The Minnehaha Engine Company, founded early and prosperous, had notable members including H.P. Grant (foreman), M.J. O’Connor, and H.B. Terwilliger. The department included several chiefs, such as Chas. H. Williams and W.T. Donaldson. In 1866, the Hope Engine Company received a steamer, but the boys of the company disbanded over the selection of its engineer, leading to the formation of St. Paul Hose Company No. 1. Jackson, a location near the fire, was also the site of a lynching in 1859. The firemen are remembered as brave relics of the past, reflecting on the dangers they faced and expressing nostalgia for the old days.

Daily newspapers seldom published on Washington's birthday, the Fourth of July, Christmas, New Year's, or Thanksgiving, especially before and after the Civil War. The Pioneer, Minnesotian, and Times were morning papers printed the evening before, with the Pioneer scooping the news of Minnesota's admission by accidentally learning it from a passenger on a late boat. In 1902, John W. Hutchinson, the last survivor of the patriotic Hutchinson family prominent in anti-bellum times, celebrated his 81st birthday in Chicago, reporting good health and planning a singing and speaking crusade against cigarette use. The Hutchinson family, known for singing their own music, visited St. Paul, named after them, where they celebrated with cannon fire, anvils, and firecrackers, holding the greatest Fourth of July celebration in history. Washington's birthday was celebrated with greater pomp than any other holiday during the anti-bellum era. John W. Hutchinson had previously spent his 75th birthday in New York, where he was received by and organized the American Temperance Union.

The Battle at Mill Springs, fought 45 years prior to the passage, was the first significant Union victory in the Southwest after the rebellion began, leading to widespread rejoicing in the loyal North. The battle ground, spanning about 3.5 miles from Pittsburg, saw Union forces positioned with their right near Crump's Landing, center facing the road to Corinth, and left extending toward Harrisburg. Gen. Lew Wallace, who took a circuitous route from Crump's Landing, appeared suddenly on the rebel left wing and had a reinforced division on the Union right, turning both wings against the enemy with the intent to drive them into an extensive ravine. The enemy retreated in excellent order, halting at advantageous points and delivering fire with considerable effect. A powerful battery on an open field fired volleys that had a telling effect on rebel ranks, with Union guns fired at 11:30, inspired by the prospect of ultimate victory. Among the surviving participants living in St. Paul are M.J. Clum, born in Rensselar County, New York, in 1832, who came to St. Paul in 1853 and worked as a printer, having learned his trade in Troy and worked with John M. Francis and C.L. McArthur.

A large car drawn by six black horses, inscribed with "Franklin," "Morse," and "Field," illustrated printers and printing in the era of Franklin and other epochs in his life. Miss Azelene Allen, a star at the People's Theater on Fourth and St. Peter Streets, represented the Goddess of Liberty with a cap on a spear and was associated with the theater alongside Miss Emily Dow and Harry Gossan. Col. R.E.J. Miles, also a theater star who first produced the play "Mazeppa" there, marched in a procession with Miss Emily Dow on caparisoned horses in Continental costume, symbolizing George and Martha Washington. The People's Theater was the only real theater in St. Paul and was managed by H. Van Liew. During a battle, the Second Minnesota and Ninth Ohio advanced in good order through a field, leading to victory despite thick mist and smoke, with a rebel lieutenant standing before the Second Minnesota. Farmers halted transport to the city due to government seizure of goods crossing the bridge and left their harvesters in the field, while their wives finished harvesting. Photography is predicted as the next great advance, eliminating printer and proofreader work.

The Mill Springs Campaign occurred from January 1 to January 17, 1862, as Gen. George H. Thomas began the operation. Union forces marched through rain, sleet, and mud, ending at Logan's Cross Roads, eight miles north of Zollicoffer's camp at Beech Grove. The gunboat Tyler fired a broadside from her immense guns, with shells tearing through the woods, spreading havoc, and striking terror into the rebel force. Rebel leaders had planned to annihilate Grant's army, cross the Tennessee River, punish Buell, and march through Tennessee, Kentucky, and into Ohio, but their bold movement failed due to sturdy resistance and heroism by Union forces. Gen. Albert Sidney Johnston was killed during the first day's battle while attempting to induce a brigade to charge. The Second Minnesota entered the woods, passed through the Tenth Indiana, ran out of ammunition, and retired, causing rebels to mistakenly believe the Union was retreating and advance to the rail fence—only to retreat themselves. By noon, rebels were retreating, making little fire, and heading toward Corinth. The Second Minnesota, along with the Eighteenth U.S. Infantry, Ninth and Thirty-fifth Ohio regiments, formed a brigade that became part of Thomas's First Division. General Grant, supported by 5,000 men from Lew Wallace's division, believed he could have driven the rebels back to Corinth. The men later proved to be some of the best soldiers in the service.

The Central House, located at the corner of Bench and Minnesota streets, was the first hotel of any pretension built in St. Paul and one of the last to be destroyed, burning in August 1873. It was converted into a large boarding house and operated by Mrs. Corbett, Mrs. Ferguson, George Pulford, and Ben Ferris before its destruction. The hotel hosted the first session of the territorial legislature of Minnesota in its dining room. The Hotel to the Wild Hunter, located on Bench Street, had a curious sign and attracted visitor attention for many years before being destroyed in a fire. The Emmert House, built by Fred Emmert on Bench Street near Wabasha, was destroyed by fire in the winter of 1868 and had previously served as a hotel and boarding house for African American families. The Merchants Hotel is the only remaining hotel on Bench Street, though only in name. The New England, a two-story log hotel, was among the ruins of the 1862 fire on Third Street above Jackson, and was historically significant as the first gubernatorial mansion where Gov. and Mrs. Ramsey began housekeeping in 1849. A spring located below the Merchants Hotel supplied water to Mr. Moore, who worked as a printer's devil for the Minnesotian in 1858.

Robert, born during a planetary conjunction predicted to bring perfect beatitude, is destined to become the mighty chief of a great city that will one day be built on land he sees. A voyageur discovers that a paleface (Robert) has arrived before him in a city stretching from the North Star State (Minnesota) to the Gulf of Mexico, where a dusky maiden delivers a prophecy stating Robert’s eternal destiny. The maiden, using fixed stars, foretells that Robert will conquer all enemies through an elixir known to her people for generations. Robert, who keeps a rod and gun, withdraws from conflict when danger arises, pursuing bison or fishing instead, and preserves friendship by avoiding convictions, allowing his friends to oppose each other on schemes. He believes votes matter more than people’s prosperity. Tom Marshall, recovering from over-indulgence in Kentucky’s moonshine, claims to have found an elixir in Minnesota at least as invigorating as Kentucky’s products. The first boat through a lake received free wharfage of $1,000.

The battle occurred on a day marked by intense fighting, with rebels flanking and capturing part of Gen. Prentiss's force. Firing continued for half an hour near the Tennessee River, shaking the ground, before ceasing by 6 o'clock as rebels withdrew. Casualties totaled three killed and six wounded, two of whom died shortly after. The "hornet's nest" saw a fierce engagement; if the First Battery had not held, Union forces would have been forced into a dangerous retreat near the river. Capt. Munch was wounded in the head and thigh, disabling him from further service, and was succeeded by Lieut. Pfaender, who lost his horse. Enemy forces drove in the pickets of Gen. Sherman's division and attacked three Ohio regiments composed of raw recruits who were unaware of the enemy's approach. The ground was contested foot by foot, with maimed soldiers falling back without help while others fought until forced back by company officers. The morning battle was re-enacted on the same ground with equal vigor on both sides.

Savannah was the destination of three companies that traveled from Fort Donelson, one of which was Capt. Shelly's Company. These companies arrived to prepare for a meeting with Gen. Beauregard, who stated he would water his horses in the Tennessee River or in hell before sundown. The gunboat Lexington, which arrived from Savannah, sent a message to Gen. Grant to determine the enemy’s direction and then positioned itself half a mile above the river landing, firing shells into a deep ravine with thick, fast gunfire that had a significant effect. After the battle, Capt. Shelly's Company was engaged for three months in protecting a railroad running from Columbus, Ky., to Corinth, Miss. Old men in a mountainous, sparsely settled area of northern Pennsylvania had served in the War of 1812 and were respected like Civil War heroes. The younger generation there began to desire knowledge, though it was difficult to obtain under prevailing conditions. The father of the Emmets, a gallant War of 1812 soldier, once lived in a brown frame house at the intersection of Ramsey and West Seventh Streets.
